popularUi.diagramDescription: Animated rule diagram for {title}: signal, player response, and recovery.

wide-swing.overview: A broad melee arc denies the space beside and in front of the boss, asking the player to leave the arc, pass through it, or exploit the unprotected side.
wide-swing.signal: Show the weapon’s start side, shoulder rotation, and intended arc before the hitbox becomes active; the pose should reveal whether the swing is high, low, or full-height.
wide-swing.response: Support at least one ordinary escape such as stepping out, moving behind the boss, or timing a dodge through the active edge, then leave a short punish window.
wide-swing.tuning: Tune reach, angular speed, active duration, and boss rotation together; test the slowest legal movement option at several starting distances.
wide-swing.pitfall: If the hitbox leads the weapon or extends far beyond it, the player learns to distrust the animation instead of reading the arc.
wide-swing.escalation: Add a delayed reverse swing or a second height only after the base arc and its safe side are readable on their own.
wide-swing.recovery: The weapon completes its arc and the boss holds the follow-through long enough for the unprotected side to become a real approach route before the stance resets.

lunge.overview: The boss commits its body along a short line to close distance, converting open space into immediate contact danger and a new final position.
lunge.signal: Use a compressed stance, fixed facing, and a clear line from the boss to the destination; lock the direction before the damaging movement begins.
lunge.response: Let the player sidestep the line, cross over it, interrupt the preparation, or bait the destination, depending on the game’s movement verbs.
lunge.tuning: Balance travel distance against preparation time and recovery; verify that the player can clear the boss’s full body, not only its center line.
lunge.pitfall: Late homing turns a readable lunge into a tracking hit and invalidates the position chosen during the tell.
lunge.escalation: Chain a second lunge toward the new position or vary the travel distance while preserving the same commitment cue.
lunge.recovery: The boss brakes at the committed destination and cannot immediately steer into another hit, giving a player who cleared the body line time to re-engage.

grab.overview: A grab replaces ordinary damage with capture, displacement, or a special follow-up, so it needs stronger communication than a routine strike.
grab.signal: Give the grab a unique hand pose, sound, and reach preview that cannot be confused with a blockable or low-damage melee attack.
grab.response: Define whether spacing, dodging, interruption, or an escape input works, and keep that rule consistent across player states and camera angles.
grab.tuning: Measure acquisition width, forward reach, tracking cutoff, escape timing, and the total consequence of failure as one package.
grab.pitfall: A grab that visually misses but snaps the player into place feels like broken collision, especially when its consequence is severe.
grab.escalation: Change what happens after capture or combine the grab with arena displacement instead of quietly increasing invisible reach.
grab.recovery: A missed grab reaches full extension and retracts visibly before another action; a successful capture uses its own explicit outcome instead of hiding the recovery.

burrow-and-emerge.overview: The boss leaves direct interaction, relocates beneath or outside the arena, and returns through a marked emergence that reshapes positioning.
burrow-and-emerge.signal: Keep an exit cue and a destination cue visible: disturbed ground, a moving trail, particles, or an arena marker should bridge the hidden interval.
burrow-and-emerge.response: The player should relocate away from the emergence zone, prepare an intercept, or use the hidden interval for a different objective.
burrow-and-emerge.tuning: Tune hidden duration, destination lock time, emergence radius, and recovery so relocation creates tension without becoming dead time.
burrow-and-emerge.pitfall: A random reappearance under the player with no trackable cue makes movement irrelevant and rewards guessing.
burrow-and-emerge.escalation: Add false trails, several possible exits, or hazards left behind while keeping the final committed destination identifiable.
burrow-and-emerge.recovery: After emergence, the ground marker dissipates and the boss finishes turning above the surface, creating a brief readable interval before tracking resumes.

ring-volley.overview: Projectiles expand from the boss in every direction, testing radial spacing and the player’s ability to find or create a route through a closing circle.
ring-volley.signal: Charge energy around the complete emitter and show any deliberate gap before launch so the player reads a ring rather than unrelated shots.
ring-volley.response: Let the player pass through a gap, move with the expanding ring, block a limited section, or interrupt the charge if that counter is intended.
ring-volley.tuning: Tune projectile count and radius growth against arena size; gaps must remain wide enough at the distance where the player is expected to cross.
ring-volley.pitfall: A ring spawned directly on the player tests reaction latency instead of radial planning.
ring-volley.escalation: Offset consecutive rings, rotate their gaps, or vary expansion speed without hiding where each safe route begins.
ring-volley.recovery: Once the expanding ring has crossed the playable route, emission stops and the boss pauses before producing another radial pattern.

spiral-barrage.overview: A rotating emitter releases a stream that traces a spiral, turning projectile timing into a moving lane the player can follow or cross.
spiral-barrage.signal: Show rotation direction, emission rhythm, and the first arm of the spiral before the pattern fills the arena.
spiral-barrage.response: The player can move with the rotation, cross one arm during a wide interval, or reposition toward a region where lane spacing is larger.
spiral-barrage.tuning: Coordinate angular velocity, fire interval, projectile speed, and duration; small changes can close every lane several seconds later.
spiral-barrage.pitfall: Tuning only the first second misses delayed overlaps that make the mature spiral impossible to navigate.
spiral-barrage.escalation: Reverse rotation, add a second offset arm, or pulse the fire rate after the player has learned the base lane motion.
spiral-barrage.recovery: The emitter stops while the mature spiral arms continue leaving the arena, preventing a new pattern from overlapping an unreadable residue.

ricochet-projectile.overview: A projectile changes direction after contacting arena boundaries, making walls part of its future trajectory and extending the threat beyond the initial shot.
ricochet-projectile.signal: Use a stable reflection rule and a visible impact cue so the next segment can be predicted from the incoming angle and surface.
ricochet-projectile.response: Players should anticipate the bounce, move to a region the reflected line will miss, or manipulate the impact point when the system permits it.
ricochet-projectile.tuning: Limit lifetime or bounce count, then test speed, collision radius, wall angles, and camera framing across every supported arena shape.
ricochet-projectile.pitfall: Random reflection angles remove the spatial reasoning that distinguishes a ricochet from an ordinary erratic projectile.
ricochet-projectile.escalation: Increase bounce count or add destructible reflectors while keeping the reflection law and projectile lifetime visible.
ricochet-projectile.recovery: The projectile expires after its advertised bounce count or lifetime with a visible fade, so reflected paths cannot remain as unbounded background danger.

homing-projectile.overview: A projectile adjusts its heading toward the player after launch, creating a moving pursuit problem instead of a single predicted line.
homing-projectile.signal: Identify lock-on and tracking strength through a marker, curved trail, or turning pose before the projectile reaches close range.
homing-projectile.response: Allow sharp direction changes, cover, interception, outrunning, or redirection according to the game’s verbs, and establish when tracking stops.
homing-projectile.tuning: Tune speed, turn rate, tracking delay, lifetime, and collision size together; a slower projectile can still be inescapable with unlimited turning.
homing-projectile.pitfall: Perfect turning with no lifetime or cutoff forces a specific exploit instead of supporting readable movement.
homing-projectile.escalation: Combine weak homing with obstacles or stagger several lock times rather than simply raising turn rate to perfect tracking.
homing-projectile.recovery: Tracking ends at a communicated cutoff and the projectile expires or travels straight, ensuring the pursuit creates a finite response window.

straight-beam.overview: The boss projects a sustained line of danger that controls a corridor and separates warning, activation, and recovery into clear timing phases.
straight-beam.signal: Draw the future line with aiming posture, light, particles, or a harmless guide before the damaging beam appears.
straight-beam.response: The player leaves the corridor, crosses before activation, uses cover, interrupts the cast, or exploits the boss’s fixed facing.
straight-beam.tuning: Measure warning time, beam width, active duration, rotation tolerance, and recovery against the distance needed to clear the whole player body.
straight-beam.pitfall: If the damaging width exceeds the preview or the beam snaps after the warning, the telegraph teaches the wrong rule.
straight-beam.escalation: Add multiple fixed lines or shorten the warning after mastery while preserving the exact relationship between preview and damage.
straight-beam.recovery: The beam shuts down along the same corridor that was previewed, and the boss keeps its facing locked for a short punish window before aiming again.

scanning-beam.overview: A sustained beam sweeps across space from one side to another, turning a line hazard into a timed crossing or pacing challenge.
scanning-beam.signal: Reveal the pivot, sweep direction, start angle, and movement speed before activation so the player can plan where to cross.
scanning-beam.response: Players can move ahead of the sweep, cross through a permitted gap, use cover, or rotate around the pivot at a safer radius.
scanning-beam.tuning: Tune angular speed, beam width, pivot position, sweep range, and arena obstructions; test inner and outer routes separately.
scanning-beam.pitfall: Changing sweep speed mid-attack without a cue invalidates the timing learned from the beam’s earlier movement.
scanning-beam.escalation: Reverse after a pause, move the pivot, or pair two scanners with offset timing while maintaining visible paths.
scanning-beam.recovery: The sweep pauses at its final angle and powers down before the pivot resets, avoiding an invisible damaging snap back to the start.

rotating-beams.overview: Two or more beam arms rotate around a source, dividing the arena into moving sectors whose spacing defines a continuous navigation rhythm.
rotating-beams.signal: Show arm count, rotation direction, and safe sector size before damage begins; all active arms should share an understandable pivot.
rotating-beams.response: The player follows a safe sector, crosses one arm at a controlled moment, or changes radius to alter the required movement speed.
rotating-beams.tuning: Coordinate arm count, angular speed, width, radius, and duration; verify that camera motion does not disguise the world-space rotation.
rotating-beams.pitfall: Too many wide arms erase the safe sector and reduce the mechanic to mandatory invulnerability frames.
rotating-beams.escalation: Change direction or arm count only at signaled breaks, giving the player time to adopt the new rhythm.
rotating-beams.recovery: The rotating arms visibly stall and fade before direction or arm count can change, giving the player a clean rhythm break.

marked-area-strike.overview: The boss marks a region first and damages it after a delay, testing whether the player can interpret shape, timing, and overlap before detonation.
marked-area-strike.signal: The marker must match the final damage footprint and communicate countdown through fill, pulse, sound, or another redundant channel.
marked-area-strike.response: Players leave the shape, choose a safe overlap, bait the mark away from useful space, or use a clearly supported defensive action.
marked-area-strike.tuning: Tune delay, footprint, placement rule, persistence, and simultaneous mark count against the player’s ordinary travel distance.
marked-area-strike.pitfall: A decorative marker that is smaller than the real hitbox makes careful positioning less reliable than panic movement.
marked-area-strike.escalation: Layer shapes with different delays or let old marks persist briefly, but keep their detonation order unmistakable.
marked-area-strike.recovery: The detonation clears its promised footprint promptly, and the boss leaves enough delay for the player to use the position chosen during the warning.

shockwave.overview: An impact creates a threat that travels across a surface, separating the boss’s strike location from the later line the player must clear.
shockwave.signal: Emphasize the source impact and the surface that will carry the wave; height and travel direction should be visible at release.
shockwave.response: The player jumps, changes elevation, blocks, moves beyond the wave’s reach, or exploits a deliberate break in the surface.
shockwave.tuning: Tune travel speed, height, lifetime, surface coverage, and repeated spacing against jump airtime and landing control.
shockwave.pitfall: A wave hidden by floor art or camera effects becomes a reaction test to an unreadable hazard.
shockwave.escalation: Alternate low and high waves, split them at obstacles, or repeat them in a learnable rhythm after the base traversal is clear.
shockwave.recovery: The wave must pass the player’s complete body before it dissipates, while the impact pose holds a short recovery that rewards a correctly timed crossing.

lingering-hazard.overview: An attack leaves danger active after the initial hit, converting a momentary threat into temporary arena control and future route planning.
lingering-hazard.signal: Distinguish the initial impact, active hazard, and expiration states so the player knows when entering the area is unsafe and when it clears.
lingering-hazard.response: Players route around the zone, bait it toward low-value space, remove it with a supported tool, or accept a clearly priced tradeoff.
lingering-hazard.tuning: Tune footprint, lifetime, placement frequency, damage cadence, and maximum simultaneous coverage as one arena budget.
lingering-hazard.pitfall: Hazards that outlive their readable visuals create invisible damage and make the arena state impossible to audit.
lingering-hazard.escalation: Let zones grow, drift, or react to other attacks while enforcing a cap that preserves at least one viable route.
lingering-hazard.recovery: The zone cools, shrinks, or fades through an unmistakable expiration state before its space becomes safe again.

hazard-trail.overview: Movement leaves a temporary dangerous path behind the boss or player, making recent trajectories constrain the next route through the arena.
hazard-trail.signal: Show where the trail begins, its exact width, and how it expires; the moving source and persistent residue need distinct visual states.
hazard-trail.response: The player curves movement to place the trail safely, crosses behind its expiration edge, or uses open space before routes close.
hazard-trail.tuning: Balance trail lifetime, width, source speed, turn radius, and arena area so route choices matter without sealing every exit.
hazard-trail.pitfall: A trail that appears behind the visual source with no placement preview punishes movement the player has already committed to.
hazard-trail.escalation: Increase persistence or add a second trail source, then cap overlap and preserve a readable expiration order.
hazard-trail.recovery: Trail segments expire in placement order and reopen the route from oldest to newest, making recovery of arena space predictable.

platform-destruction.overview: The boss removes or disables pieces of traversable space, making arena geometry a changing resource rather than a fixed backdrop.
platform-destruction.signal: Cracks, deformation, targeted highlights, and sound should identify the exact platform and whether its loss is temporary or permanent.
platform-destruction.response: Players relocate before collapse, choose which space to sacrifice, use alternate traversal, or complete an objective before the route disappears.
platform-destruction.tuning: Track remaining safe area, route connectivity, destruction order, recovery options, and the abilities required to survive each layout.
platform-destruction.pitfall: Removing the only reachable platform after an earlier irreversible choice creates a soft lock instead of meaningful pressure.
platform-destruction.escalation: Destroy space in authored stages or allow restoration between cycles, ensuring every state has a tested route for the intended loadout.
platform-destruction.recovery: The surviving layout stabilizes before the next attack; if platforms return, restoration is signaled and finishes before they become required routes.

shrinking-safe-area.overview: Danger advances inward or outward to reduce usable space, increasing contact pressure and forcing the encounter toward a tighter final layout.
shrinking-safe-area.signal: Show the future boundary, direction of travel, and final stopping point before it moves; the safe side must remain unambiguous.
shrinking-safe-area.response: The player repositions early, finishes a task before compression, controls where other hazards land, or uses a temporary opening to cross.
shrinking-safe-area.tuning: Tune boundary speed, minimum safe area, pause intervals, other attack footprints, and camera framing at every shrink stage.
shrinking-safe-area.pitfall: Continuous compression with no stable interval denies the player time to understand or use the new arena state.
shrinking-safe-area.escalation: Shrink in discrete, signaled steps or shift the safe center while preserving enough space for the next required response.
shrinking-safe-area.recovery: The boundary stops at the announced minimum size and holds a stable interval so the player can understand and use the compressed arena.

knockback.overview: A hit displaces the player, so its real danger depends on nearby walls, ledges, hazards, and the loss of a chosen position.
knockback.signal: Communicate push direction and strength through the boss pose, impact line, and arena context before the force resolves.
knockback.response: Players brace, move away from dangerous boundaries, steer during displacement, use immunity, or deliberately take a safe push for repositioning.
knockback.tuning: Evaluate force, stun time, air control, collision behavior, and every possible landing zone rather than balancing damage alone.
knockback.pitfall: A small-looking hit that launches the player farther than the arena reads makes environmental deaths feel arbitrary.
knockback.escalation: Combine moderate push with changing boundary hazards or directional choices instead of scaling force until recovery is impossible.
knockback.recovery: The player regains control before the next unavoidable threat while the boss completes its follow-through, preserving recovery from a safe landing.

target-lock.overview: The boss selects a player or position, communicates that selection, and commits a later attack to it, creating a window for deliberate placement.
target-lock.signal: Use a persistent marker and a clear lock moment that distinguishes tracking before commitment from the fixed target after commitment.
target-lock.response: The marked player moves the attack away, shares or transfers responsibility if supported, or waits for commitment before leaving the area.
target-lock.tuning: Tune selection range, tracking duration, lock delay, attack delay, and multiplayer priority rules so responsibility remains legible.
target-lock.pitfall: Continuing to retarget after the lock cue teaches players that the marker has no dependable meaning.
target-lock.escalation: Lock several targets, attach different outcomes to markers, or shorten the placement window while keeping commitment explicit.
target-lock.recovery: The marker is consumed at the committed location and cannot follow the player after lock; a short reset separates that resolution from the next selection.

attack-combination.overview: Two or more familiar attacks are sequenced so the first response changes the starting conditions for the next, creating a composite decision.
attack-combination.signal: Preserve the tells of each component and add a rhythm or stance that communicates whether the sequence will continue.
attack-combination.response: The player chooses a first answer that also leaves space, resources, and facing for the known follow-up rather than solving each hit in isolation.
attack-combination.tuning: Tune transition gaps, positional carryover, cancellation rules, and total sequence duration; test every legal response to the opening move.
attack-combination.pitfall: Combining individually fair attacks can still create an unavoidable follow-up if the first recovery ends in the second danger zone.
attack-combination.escalation: Branch the final move from a small set of clearly signaled options after the fixed opening sequence is learned.
attack-combination.recovery: After the final component, the boss enters a recovery proportional to the combined coverage instead of chaining immediately into a fresh sequence.

weak-point.overview: Damage is concentrated on a specific body part, state, or facing, turning access to the target into a positioning and timing objective.
weak-point.signal: Use shape, material, animation, and hit feedback to distinguish the vulnerable region and show when it opens or closes.
weak-point.response: Players reposition, provoke an exposing attack, break protection, or reserve high-value actions for the vulnerability window.
weak-point.tuning: Tune access frequency, window length, damage multiplier, target size, camera visibility, and support for different attack ranges.
weak-point.pitfall: A weak point that visually reads as exposed but rejects valid hits makes the vulnerability rule feel inconsistent.
weak-point.escalation: Move the weak point, link it to a breakable part, or require alternating access routes while preserving clear open and closed feedback.
weak-point.recovery: The exposed point closes with a visible guard or state change, and the boss does not accept hidden weak-point hits after the window ends.

telegraph.overview: A telegraph communicates an upcoming attack’s timing, origin, direction, and footprint early enough for a meaningful response.
telegraph.signal: Coordinate pose, motion, sound, effects, and arena markers so at least two channels identify the same future event without visual clutter.
telegraph.response: The player should be able to convert the cue into a specific action—move, wait, interrupt, guard, or prepare—before commitment removes that choice.
telegraph.tuning: Tune recognition time separately from movement time, then test cue visibility at combat distance, under effects, and with reduced audio or color perception.
telegraph.pitfall: A long animation is not a useful telegraph if it does not reveal what space becomes dangerous or when commitment occurs.
telegraph.escalation: Shorten or partially share tells only after the base vocabulary is established, preserving one reliable discriminator for each outcome.
telegraph.recovery: The damaging action resolves in exactly the promised shape, then a clear cooldown separates its result from the next warning.

fight-phase.overview: A health, time, or objective threshold changes the encounter’s rules, moves, arena, or goals to create a distinct stage of the same fight.
fight-phase.signal: Mark the transition with a pause, animation, music change, camera beat, or environment shift that clearly separates old and new rules.
fight-phase.response: Give the player a moment to read the new state, reposition, or change priorities before the first unfamiliar threat fully resolves.
fight-phase.tuning: Balance phase length, transition safety, retained hazards, resource state, checkpoints, and how quickly the new rule is introduced.
fight-phase.pitfall: Changing several rules during an unprotected attack can make the first failure feel like missing information rather than a design challenge.
fight-phase.escalation: Recombine mastered mechanics or change the immediate objective in later phases instead of only increasing health and damage.
fight-phase.recovery: The transition ends only after the new arena, objective, and boss state are stable, with a short onboarding beat before the next full-pressure action.

enrage.overview: The boss enters a more demanding state after a threshold or time limit, raising pressure and establishing a clear late-fight climax.
enrage.signal: Use a distinct transition and persistent state cue so players know which speeds, sequences, or recovery rules have changed.
enrage.response: The player adapts positioning and resource use to the announced changes while retaining at least one dependable answer to every attack.
enrage.tuning: Choose the trigger, speed increase, damage change, new moves, and recovery reduction independently; avoid multiplying every value at once.
enrage.pitfall: Removing all punish windows during enrage turns mastery into attrition and can invalidate builds that rely on deliberate counterattacks.
enrage.escalation: Add one new rule or compress selected timings, then preserve the visual grammar learned earlier so the climax remains readable.
enrage.recovery: The transformation finishes with a readable reset before the accelerated cycle begins; the stronger state persists instead of flickering between attacks.
